title: Checkpoint: Reading Telugu
summary: A cumulative examination of sections four to six: the vowel signs and the guṇintam, the pollu and the subjoined consonants, the digits, and the verbless sentence. By the end of it a learner can read a Telugu word aloud and say what it means.

drills.stem: Which of these is read *mā*?
drills.explanation: The sign ా to the right of మ replaces the inherent అ with ā. మ alone is *ma*; మి and ము carry different signs.

drills.stem: Which vowel is written with **no sign at all**?
drills.explanation: అ needs none — it is already inside every consonant. Fifteen of the sixteen vowels have signs, and this is the one that does not.

drills.stem: Which of these is read *nadi*?
drills.explanation: The first consonant bears no sign and keeps అ; the second has the i-sign. నాది and నదీ lengthen the wrong vowel; నిది puts i on the first letter.

drills.stem: Which of these signs are written **below** the consonant?
drills.explanation: ు and ూ hang below. ే sits above and ా is written to the right — the three positions that make the syllable, and not the mark, the unit of reading.

drills.stem: Why are **ఉ** and **ు** two shapes for one vowel?
options: They are different vowels transliterated alike.
ఉ is written where no consonant precedes; ు is written on a consonant.
drills.explanation: One vowel, two situations: the independent letter for the start of a word, the sign for everywhere else. Every vowel but అ has both shapes.

drills.stem: How many **vowel signs** must be learned in all, given that every consonant uses the same set?
drills.explanation: Fifteen: sixteen vowels less అ. Those fifteen marks unlock all thirty-six guṇintams at once, which is why they repay study more than the letters do.

drills.stem: A learner has memorised all fifty-two letters and still cannot read a printed page. Why most likely?
options: Printed Telugu uses a different alphabet.
Several vowel signs reshape the top of the consonant, so the letters on the page do not match those on the chart.
The words are printed right to left.
The letters are in a different order on the page.
drills.explanation: క, కి and కె are one consonant in three dresses (¶26). The chart teaches thirty-six shapes; the page shows each of them in sixteen.

drills.stem: What does the **పొల్లు** do to a consonant?
options: It takes away its inherent vowel.
drills.explanation: క is *ka*, క్ is *k*. It is the only way to write a bare consonant, and it is what other Indian scripts call the virāma.

drills.stem: Which digit is *seven*?
drills.explanation: ౭ is seven. The four digits sit in order from five to eight.

drills.stem: Two consonants meet inside a word with no vowel between them. How is that written?
options: With a pollu on the first.
With the second subjoined beneath the first, as an ఒత్తు.
With a vowel sign on each.
drills.explanation: The pollu belongs chiefly to the end of a word; within one, the two consonants are joined into a single written unit. The anusvāra does the work only where the first is a nasal of the second's varga.

drills.stem: Why is a subjoined consonant hard to recognise?
options: It stands for a different sound from the full letter.
It is reduced and loses its తలకట్టు, so it no longer matches the chart.
It is written above the letter.
It is written in a different script.
drills.explanation: The sound is unchanged; only the shape is reduced. Learning the thirty-six ottu forms is a second labour after learning the thirty-six letters.

drills.stem: Which of these words contain a **doubled** consonant?
drills.explanation: ఇల్లు has ll and అమ్మ has mm, each written as a letter conjoined with itself and each held longer in speech. నది and పులి have plain consonants with vowels between them.

drills.stem: In **పుస్తకం**, what does the పొల్లు under **స్** mark?
options: That స carries the vowel అ.
That స has no vowel of its own before త.
drills.explanation: The pollu under స removes its inherent అ so that స and త meet as a cluster. Without it the word would be read with an extra vowel.

drills.stem: How is **four hundred and two** written in Telugu digits?
drills.explanation: ౪ ౦ ౨ — four, zero, two — left to right. The third option reverses the digits; the second swaps the last two.

drills.stem: Which statements about the pollu and the ottu are correct?
options: Both remove a vowel between two consonants.
The ottu is used chiefly inside a word, the pollu chiefly at its end.
A consonant written as an ottu keeps its full shape.
The pollu is what other Indian scripts call the virāma.
drills.explanation: The ottu is reduced and loses its headstroke — precisely what makes conjuncts hard to read. The two devices solve one problem in two positions.

drills.stem: Translate: **That is a house.**
drills.explanation: అది is *that* and ఇది *this*; no verb is written, and కాదు would deny the statement instead of making it.

drills.stem: How is **ఇది పుస్తకం** denied?
options: By putting కాదు at the end.
By putting కాదు at the beginning.
By adding a verb and negating it.
drills.explanation: One word added at the end, and nothing already there altered. There is no verb in the sentence to negate.

drills.stem: Which of these phrases are **correctly** formed?
drills.explanation: The adjective stands before its noun and never changes form. Only the third reverses the order.

drills.stem: Which word asks **what**, of a thing?
drills.explanation: ఏమిటి asks what; ఎవరు asks who, of a person. అక్కడ is "there" and అవును "yes".

drills.stem: **ఇది మంచి ఇల్లు.** If this became a denial, how many of its three words would change form?
drills.explanation: None. కాదు is added at the end and nothing already present is altered — the adjective is invariable, the nouns unmarked, and there is no verb to negate.

drills.title: నా ఇల్లు
drills.passage: ఇది నా ఇల్లు. ఇది పెద్ద ఇల్లు కాదు. ఇక్కడ నా పుస్తకం. అది మంచి పుస్తకం. అక్కడ నా అన్న. అతని పేరు రవి. అతను మంచి అన్న.
drills.translation: This is my house. This is not a big house. Here is my book. That is a good book. There is my elder brother. His name is Ravi. He is a good brother.

questions.explanation: *అతని పేరు రవి.* *అన్న* says what he is — an elder brother — not what he is called.
*ఇక్కడ నా పుస్తకం* — the book is here. అక్కడ is where the brother is.

questions.stem: How many verbs does the passage contain?
questions.explanation: None. Seven statements, every one an equation of two nouns, and not a verb among them — the most surprising fact about elementary Telugu for a speaker of a European language.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985.

drills.stem: Match each Telugu sentence with what it says. One entry in Column II is used by none of them.
drills.explanation: కాదు at the end denies the identity; ఏమిటి asks what, not who. The second option swaps the affirmation with its denial; the third gives ఏమిటి to who; the fourth swaps house with what.
